pugnacious.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pugnāci-, a stem of pugnax (“fond of fighting, aggressive, combative, pugnacious”) + English -ous (“suffix forming adjectives from nouns…
pugnacious.x: Plato affirms Idees; / But Ariſtotle vvith his pugnacious race / As idle figments ſtifly them denies.

pulchritude.e: From Middle English pulcritude, from Latin pulchritūdō, from pulcher (“beautiful”).
pulchritude.x: Do you know why a woman of such pulchritude is married to me? 'Cause I make a comfortable living.

pullet.e: From Middle English polet, pulet, from Anglo-Norman pullet, Old French poulet (“young chicken”).
pullet.x: They died not because the Pullets would not feed: but because the Devil foresaw their death, he contrived that abstinence in them.

pulley.e: Inherited from Middle English puly, poley, from Old French poulie, polie (“a pulley, windlass”), from Vulgar Latin *polidia, plural mistaken for the feminine of neuter…

pullover.x: I followed my training in the academy regarding vehicle pullovers.

pulmonary.e: Borrowed from Latin pulmōnārius (“of the lungs”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ārius, from Proto-Indo-European *pléu-mon-.

pulpit.e: From Middle English pulpit, from Old French pulpite and Latin pulpitum (“platform”). Doublet of pulpitum and polypus. Piecewise doublet of polypod.
pulpit.x: He seems like too timid a man to fill the pulpit at such a large church.

pulsar.e: Blend of pulsating + (radio) star, patterned after quasar. Coined by British astronomers Antony Hewish and Jocelyn Bell in 1968, and first used in print in The Daily…

pulsate.e: Perhaps formed within English as a back-formation from pulsation (attested from the early 15th century, in Middle English).

pulverise.e: From Middle English pulverizen, from Latin pulverizō, pulverizāre, from pulvis (“powder”). Compare French pulvériser. By surface analysis, pulver (“powder”) + -ise.

pummel.x: The politician was pummeled by the media for his controversial statements.

punctual.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis (adjective suffix).
punctual.x: Luis is never late; he's the most punctual person I know.

punctuation.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (“to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + -ion.
punctuation.x: Different languages have different rules for punctuation.

puncture.x: There were two small punctures in his arm where the snake's fangs had pierced the skin.

pundit.x: This week we introduce Jenny Walker, who will be The Observer's expert pundit for the duration of the World Cup.

pungent.e: Borrowed from Latin pungens (stem pungent-), present participle of pungo (“to sting”). Doublet of poignant.
pungent.x: I accidentally dropped the bottle of ammonia and after few seconds, a very pungent stench could be detected.

punishable.x: Littering in this area is punishable by a fine of up to $100.

punitive.e: From Middle French punitif, from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).
punitive.x: Beijing imposed punitive sanctions on Canada.

pupil.e: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).
pupil.x: All of these different methods of teaching elementary reading were successful for some pupils, unsuccessful for others.

purchase.e: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”).
purchase.x: They offer a free hamburger with the purchase of a drink.

purdah.e: Borrowed from Hindustani پردہ / पर्दा (pardā), and its etymon Classical Persian پرده (pardah, “curtain; screen.

purification.e: From Old French purificacion, from Latin pūrificātiō.

purify.e: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).
purify.x: The modern arts deviate from the standards set forth by the divine—art should be used to purify one’s heart and improve one’s morality.

purist.e: Borrowed from French puriste. By surface analysis, pur(e) + -ist.
purist.x: He was the first to play for money, a practice which got him ousted from the purist U.S. Lawn Tennis Association.

purity.x: The purity of the water was tested in a laboratory.

purloin.e: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.
purloin.x: Had from his wakeful custody purloined / The guarded gold.

purposely.e: From Middle English purposly; equivalent to purpose + -ly.
purposely.x: I purposely left the door unlocked.

purslane.e: From Old French porcelaine, probably an alteration of Latin porcilaca (“purslane”) (related to portulaca (“purslane”)) to assimilate it with porcelaine (“porcelain”).

pursuant.e: Anglo-Norman pursuant, present participle of pursure. Doublet of pursuivant.
pursuant.x: And pursuant to this idea of a holiday, he insisted upon playing cards after we had eaten.

pursue.e: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.
pursue.x: He now feared for his life, and believed US intelligence agents would pursue him.

pursuit.e: From Middle English pursuyte, from Old French poursuite, from the verb porsuir (“to pursue”).
pursuit.x: Unremitting pursuit of wealth doesn't bring happiness, particularly if successful.

purulent.e: Borrowed from Middle French purulent, from Latin pūrulentus, from pūs (“pus”).
purulent.x: Close-up of two rats gnawing at a mutton bone, of the flies on the purulent eyelids of a small girl.

pusillanimous.x: The soldier deserted his troop in a pusillanimous manner.

putrid.x: Quake guzzell dogs, that live on putrid slime.

putsch.e: Borrowed from German Putsch, from Alemannic German Putsch (“knock, thrust, blow”), of imitative origin.
putsch.x: Afterward, the ringleaders of the failed putsch were publicly executed.

putty.e: Borrowed from French potée (“polishing powder", originally "the contents of a pot, potful”), from French pot (“pot”). More at English pot.

puzzled.x: They could not, it was said, keep Scandinavian bogies and the Scriptures separate in their puzzled brains.

pygmy.e: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a legendary race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”).

pylon.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πυλών (pulṓn, “gateway”).
pylon.x: After two pylonless months, July's pylon comes all the way from the hills outside Wellington, New Zealand.

pylorus.e: From Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).

pyramid.e: From French pyramide, from Old French piramide, from Latin pȳramis, pȳramidis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), possibly from πῡρός (pūrós, “wheat”) + ἀμάω (amáō…
pyramid.x: The company was organized as a pyramid, with a CEO in charge of four directors, each heading up a department.

pyramidal.e: From Middle English piramidal, piramydale, from Medieval Latin pȳramidālis. By surface analysis, pyramid + -al.

pyrite.x: The pyrite output in 1961 was 1.2 million tons, derived mainly from the Hsiang Shan mine in Anhwei and the Ying-te mine in Kwangtung.

pyrotechnics.x: Dazzling verbal pyrotechnics and incredibly vivid characterization.
